title: Rate Limiting Edge Cases
description: Handle edge cases in rate limiting including whitelisting, tiered limits, distributed clock skew, and abuse prevention.

data.text: Rate limiting looks simple on paper but has many edge cases in production: clock skew between servers, key enumeration, abuse through distributed clients, and the dilemma of limiting vs availability. This lesson covers the hard problems.

rows: Use server-provided time or NTP sync
Authenticate users; rate limit by user, not IP
Weight by response size or endpoint cost
Add jitter to reset times or smooth refill
Multiple users share an API key
Rate limit per key; warn on key sharing
Fail open or fail closed with clear policy

data.text: Not all clients are equal. Free tier users get 100 req/min, Pro users get 10,000 req/min, and Enterprise users get custom limits. Implement tiered rate limits using a tier field in the rate limit key.

data.title: Redis key design for tiered rate limits
data.content: Include the tier in the key to avoid cross-tier interference.
data.code:
# User in free tier
rate:user:123:free        -> limit: 100/min

# User in pro tier
rate:user:123:pro         -> limit: 10000/min

# Tier lookup
GET user:123
tier: "pro"

# Apply correct limit based on tier
rate:user:123:pro  => limit 10000/min
rate:user:123:free => limit 100/min

data.text: Not all requests cost the same. A GET /health should not consume the same tokens as POST /search or GET /export. Weight expensive operations by a cost factor.

data.title: Applying cost factors in the rate limit script
data.content: Pass the endpoint cost as an argument to the Lua script.
data.code:
function allowRequestWeighted(key, capacity, refillRate, now, cost)
    local bucket = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'last')
    local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or capacity
    local last = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now

    local elapsed = math.max(0, now - last) / 1000
    tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillRate)

    if tokens >= cost then
        redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens - cost, 'last', now)
        redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / refillRate))
        return {1, math.floor(tokens - cost)}
    end

    return {0, 0, math.ceil((cost - tokens) / refillRate)}
end

# Usage:
# GET /health -> cost = 0 (free)
# GET /search -> cost = 2
# GET /export -> cost = 10

data.text: Rate limit accuracy depends on all servers agreeing on the current time. Clock skew can cause early resets or overly strict limits. Use NTP, and for extreme accuracy, derive time from Redis itself (Redis returns its server time with TIME command).

items: Use NTP with a 1ms sync interval on all gateway servers
For Redis-based limiters, use the Redis TIME command instead of server clock
Allow a small skew tolerance (100-500ms) when comparing timestamps
Log time differences between server and Redis for debugging

data.text: Rate limiting alone does not stop abuse. Combine it with other signals.

items: CAPTCHA after 3 consecutive 429s from the same IP
IP reputation scoring using threat intelligence feeds
Behavioral analysis: rapid fire requests from new accounts are suspicious
Email/SMS verification before raising rate limits on new accounts
Device fingerprinting to detect distributed attacks from the same device

data.title: Rate limiting by IP is not enough
data.text: Attackers use cloud IPs, VPNs, and botnets to distribute requests across thousands of IPs. Authenticated rate limiting by user ID is the only reliable defense. IP rate limiting is a secondary layer for unauthenticated abuse.

items.question: Should I use a fuzzy time window to smooth resets?
items.answer: Token bucket already smooths resets by refilling continuously. For fixed window, add 10-20% jitter to the reset time so not all clients reset simultaneously.

items.question: How do I handle WebSocket connections?
items.answer: Rate limit the HTTP upgrade request and the WebSocket message rate separately. Message rate limiting uses a token bucket keyed by user ID, not connection ID.

items.question: What is the cost of rate limiting at scale?
items.answer: Redis handles 100K+ ops/sec per node. A token bucket with Lua costs ~2 round-trips per request (HMGET + HMSET). At 50K req/sec, you need a Redis cluster with 3+ shards.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Use tiered limits and cost-weighted requests for fair resource allocation.
Derive time from Redis to eliminate clock skew.
Rate limit by authenticated user ID, not IP.
Combine rate limiting with abuse signals: CAPTCHA, IP reputation, behavior analysis.
data.takeaway: Rate limiting edge cases are where production differs from tutorials. Weight requests by cost, tier users fairly, and never trust IP alone to stop a determined attacker.
